title: The World Cup Starts Tomorrow. The Opening Ceremony Starts Ninety Minutes Before That.
excerpt: Shakira in Mexico City. Katy Perry in LA. A 19-year-old from Kannur playing in Santa Clara. Here is everything happening in the first 48 hours.
body:
The first ball of the 2026 FIFA World Cup will be kicked at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City on Thursday, June 11, at 1:30 PM ET. Mexico will face South Africa. Ninety minutes before that, Shakira and Burna Boy will perform "Dai Dai," the tournament's official anthem, in front of 87,000 people inside a stadium that has hosted two World Cup finals before this one.

For the 4.4 million Indian Americans living across the United States, this is the first World Cup in their backyard. And for the first time, the opening is not one ceremony but three.

## Three cities, three nights

Mexico City goes first. The Estadio Azteca ceremony on Thursday features Shakira, Burna Boy, J Balvin, Tyla, Alejandro Fernandez, Danny Ocean, Lila Downs, Los Angeles Azules, Belinda, and Maná. The opening match — Mexico vs South Africa — follows immediately at 3 PM ET.

Toronto takes over on Friday. Alanis Morissette headlines a lineup that includes Michael Bublé, Alessia Cara, and Jessie Reyez. Canada kicks off their campaign against Cameroon at BMO Field later that evening.

The festivities close Friday night at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, where Katy Perry headlines alongside Future, Anitta, and LISA. The United States opens against Paraguay at 9 PM ET in what is expected to be the most-watched World Cup match in American broadcast history.

## What NRIs should watch

The group stage runs from June 11 to July 2, with 48 teams playing 104 matches across 16 cities. For diaspora fans, the matches that matter most go beyond the opening day.

**Qatar vs Switzerland on June 13 in Santa Clara** is the one circled in Bay Area calendars. Qatar's squad includes 19-year-old Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid, born in Doha to parents from Kannur, Kerala. He will play his first World Cup match at Levi's Stadium, less than an hour from the largest concentration of Indian Americans in the country. Tickets for the Qatar match were among the fastest-selling in the Bay Area allocation.

New Zealand's Sarpreet Singh, born in Auckland to Punjabi parents from Jalandhar, is confirmed in the All Whites' 26-man squad. His group-stage matches include games in Philadelphia and Seattle. Singh, who once played for Bayern Munich's first team, has spoken openly about what the tournament means. "I don't say it's added pressure. I just want to do my best to lift the names of Indian people, and there is no better stage to do it than the World Cup," he told The Mint.

Australia's Nishan Velupillay, a Melbourne Victory winger of Sri Lankan Tamil and Anglo-Indian descent, and DR Congo's Samuel Moutoussamy, who traces his roots to southern India through Guadeloupe, round out a quartet of Indian-origin players across four different nations — the most ever at a single World Cup.

## The numbers

This is the largest World Cup ever staged. Forty-eight teams, up from 32. Sixteen host cities, up from eight at the last edition in Qatar. The group stage features 12 groups of four, with the top two and eight best third-placed teams advancing to a round of 32. Every match from the round of 32 onward is single-elimination.

For NRIs, the broadcast setup matters. In the US, Fox holds the English-language rights, while Telemundo and Peacock carry Spanish-language coverage. The opening ceremony streams live on Peacock starting at 1:30 PM ET on Thursday.

## Why this one is different

India has never qualified for the World Cup. That has not changed. But for the first time, the tournament is being played in cities where millions of Indian Americans live, work, and watch. The group-stage schedule includes matches in Houston, Dallas, Atlanta, the Bay Area, Los Angeles, New York, and Seattle — every major NRI metro except Chicago.

When Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid walks out at Levi's Stadium on June 13, he will not be wearing blue. But for a 19-year-old from a Malayali family playing football's biggest tournament in Silicon Valley, the story writes itself.

The World Cup starts tomorrow. For NRIs, home advantage has never been closer.

*Sources: NBC Sports, Bleacher Report, Sporting News, The Mint, FIFA.com*
